![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/aac27058402f89bef73700129a7812b3cf4f971c11975fc1711a46b8d10e61fe.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/e2d914cf61af684d1f2971ec680acc1a2a53a6a40c85e387728dfea8ebc94730.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-2+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x+2{z}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(2{z}^{2}-2)x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{z}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(x+2{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(x+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2x{z}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(\frac{3}{2}+18) \\  & =-\frac{39}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{27}{2}+(-\frac{39}{2}) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$
